summary.text: A 77-year-old man with no known medical history and no diabetes presented to the ED with one month of worsening altered mental status, incoherence, decreased oral intake and bedbound status, and was thin and cachectic and not oriented on examination.

Vital signs were reported normal; blood counts, chemistry, renal and liver function were unremarkable; head CT and brain MRI were negative for an acute event and inflammation; CSF had 1 wbc/mm^3 and protein 31 mg/dL with negative cultures and viral/fungal studies. A serum autoimmune encephalitis panel sent on day two found VGKC antibody 142 pmol/L (the single positive antibody), with LGI1 and CASPR2 negative.

Treatment on high suspicion for autoimmune encephalitis was methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV daily for five days and IVIG 400 mg/kg/day for five days, with rituximab 375 mg/m2 added after the VGKC result; he slowly improved and by hospital day 40 followed commands and walked with a walker.

Repeat testing 61 days after the first showed VGKC 71 pmol/L and newly detected GAD antibody 37.6 IU/mL (first GAD normal) without any stiff person syndrome signs; a third-round test was not done. He was transferred to a skilled nursing facility, was home and generally independent at six months, and was alert, oriented x2, ambulatory and independent at an unrelated ED visit eighteen months later.

summary.text: A 43-year-old woman with obesity and type 2 diabetes presented to the ED with sudden right facial twitching and involuntary right eyelid spasm, with right blepharospasm, right hemifacial spasms and myokymia; vitals were stable, extraocular movements intact, brain CT/MRI negative, CSF 10 wbc/mm3 (lymphocytic predominant) with protein 23 mg/dL. She had three weeks of insomnia and developed hallucinations and disorientation a few days after admission.

Under a working diagnosis of Morvan syndrome she received oral clonazepam, methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV for five days and IVIG 400 mg/kg/day for five days; the first serum panel showed VGKC 58 and a low amphiphysin level with GAD <5. Symptoms improved two weeks after admission and she was discharged home after one month, with facial spasms still visible.

About six months later she returned with worse facial spasms and blepharospasm; repeat VGKC was 86 pmol/L, amphiphysin not detected and GAD positive at 70.7 IU/mL. She received methylprednisolone, IVIG and rituximab, baclofen was added, symptoms improved and she was discharged after three weeks.

Six months later a minor flare with facial and body pain was treated with another five-day methylprednisolone and IVIG course with improvement; the third panel showed VGKC 34 pmol/L, GAD <5 IU/mL and no detectable amphiphysin. A call three months later found minor symptoms but good function; the authors state a full return to baseline did not occur.

summary.text: A 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, after two prior ED visits elsewhere without diagnosis, came to the ED with two weeks of headaches, fevers and altered mental status; she was oriented only to name with active hallucinations, temperature 100 F, BP 156/89 mmHg, and non-revealing cranial nerve, motor, sensory and cerebellar examinations.

Brain CT and MRI were negative; CSF showed 3 wbc/mm3, protein 44 mg/dL and HSV 1/2 IgG 1.38 IV with negative IgM, and IV acyclovir was given. The ARUP autoimmune encephalitis panel was positive for VGKC at 42 pmol/L with GAD <5 IU/mL and LGI1/CASPR2 negative. She received methylprednisolone, IVIG and rituximab (timing relative to the VGKC result not stated).

Her mental status greatly improved over a few weeks and she was discharged home; per family she was back to baseline three months later. One year later she returned with acute encephalopathy likely secondary to a UTI; repeat CSF (WBC 0, protein 47 mg/dL, HSV IgG 1.63 IV) and MRI were negative, she recovered with antibiotics, was discharged after three days and received no immunomodulation.

Results returned weeks after discharge, 367 days after the original test, showed VGKC 91 pmol/L and GAD positive at 134.5 IU/mL; a third-round test was not done. A telephone follow-up found her back at baseline.

article_limitations: Caption-layer visual status not_inspected; actual figure pixels inspected in the separate visual submission.

Three-patient series; the roster is the three presented cases. Literature cases cited in the discussion (cerebral palsy case with dual VGKC/GAD positivity, limbic encephalitis case, 18-year GAD65 case, Malter et al. cohort) are background and not assigned to any patient.
Antibody names in the case text appear as "ILI-2", "LASPR2" and "CASPR-2"; abstract and discussion state LGI1 and CASPR2 negativity, and the facts record the written forms with that note.
UNIT CONFLICT: Patient 2 first VGKC value is printed as 58 pmol/dL in the narrative and 58 pmol/L in Table 1; the value is kept with the Table 1 unit and the conflict is noted.

Table 1 reference column gives VGKC categories (negative <31, intermediate 32-87, positive >88 pmol/L) that disagree with narrative labels for Patient 3 (42 called positive) and with "normal" for Patient 2 third value 34; text flags are used only where the text states them and no flag is derived from reference ranges.
Heart rate, blood pressure (Patients 1-2 and heart rate for Patient 3) and Table 1 values 34 and CSF "1" lack stated units in places; none were supplied beyond the narrative.
Symptom onset and some timings are retrospective or unanchored ("Eighteen months later", "six months later"); no dates or intervals were computed.

Authors state GAD antibodies emerged without relapse or new neurological symptoms, which sits in tension with Patient 2 flare-up and Patient 3 encephalopathy at the GAD-positive testing; both are preserved without resolution.
